h: Henry VIII's paint job and prisoners' graffiti
p: That Round Table has had a makeover or two in its time. The wood dates from around the 1270s, but the paintwork you see today was added for Henry VIII in the early sixteenth century. Take a proper look at the figure of King Arthur at the top: he's given a face that's thought to resemble a young Henry, and there's a big Tudor rose slap bang in the centre. It's a brilliant bit of royal spin, linking the Tudors to the greatest legend in British history.

The hall itself was built in the early thirteenth century under Henry III, and it has hosted some dramatic trials. Sir Walter Raleigh was tried for treason here in 1603, and in 1685 the notorious Judge Jeffreys sentenced Dame Alice Lisle in the hall during the Bloody Assizes. Look out too for the bronze statue of Queen Victoria by Alfred Gilbert, which stands inside.

Over at the Westgate, the stonework hides some fascinating details. For a time the gate was used as a debtors' prison, and inmates scratched graffiti into the walls that you can still spot today. There's also a painted ceiling made around the time Mary I married Philip of Spain in Winchester Cathedral in 1554. Climb up to the roof and you get a smashing view down the High Street.
An hour or so covers both comfortably.

From there it's an easy walk down the High Street to the cathedral, where Jane Austen is buried. Carry on to the statue of King Alfred on the Broadway, the ruins of Wolvesey Castle, the old bishops' palace, and the National Trust's working City Mill on the river. For a lovely riverside stroll, follow the water meadows out to the medieval Hospital of St Cross.
